claim: Haptic perception synthesizes touch with proprioception, the sense of body position.
source: Haptic perception synthesizes touch with proprioception, the sense of body position.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about haptic perception.

claim: Humans and mice alike experience rich active touch of the face.
source: Humans and mice alike experience rich active touch of the face.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge about sensory systems in humans and mice.

claim: Most facial muscles lack proprioceptor endings.
source: Because most facial muscles lack proprioceptor endings, the sensory basis of facial proprioception remains unsolved.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about facial muscle anatomy.

claim: The sensory basis of facial proprioception remains unsolved.
source: Because most facial muscles lack proprioceptor endings, the sensory basis of facial proprioception remains unsolved.
evidence: This is presented as a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: Facial proprioception may rely on mechanoreceptors that encode both touch and self-motion.
source: Facial proprioception may instead rely on mechanoreceptors that encode both touch and self-motion.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: In rodents, whisker mechanoreceptors provide a signal that informs the brain about whisker position.
source: In rodents, whisker mechanoreceptors provide a signal that informs the brain about whisker position.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about rodent whisker mechanoreceptors.

claim: Whisking involves coordinated orofacial movements.
source: Whisking involves coordinated orofacial movements, so mechanoreceptors innervating facial regions other than whiskers could also provide information about whisking.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about whisking behavior.

claim: Mechanoreceptors innervating facial regions other than whiskers could provide information about whisking.
source: Whisking involves coordinated orofacial movements, so mechanoreceptors innervating facial regions other than whiskers could also provide information about whisking.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the coordinated nature of whisking movements.

claim: Whisker motion was encoded best by whisker mechanoreceptors.
source: Whisker motion was encoded best by whisker mechanoreceptors, but also by those innervating whisker pad hairy skin and supraorbital vibrissae.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Whisker motion was also encoded by mechanoreceptors innervating whisker pad hairy skin.
source: Whisker motion was encoded best by whisker mechanoreceptors, but also by those innervating whisker pad hairy skin and supraorbital vibrissae.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Whisker motion was also encoded by mechanoreceptors innervating supraorbital vibrissae.
source: Whisker motion was encoded best by whisker mechanoreceptors, but also by those innervating whisker pad hairy skin and supraorbital vibrissae.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Redundant self-motion responses may provide the brain with a stable proprioceptive signal despite mechanical perturbations during active touch.
source: Redundant self-motion responses may provide the brain with a stable proprioceptive signal despite mechanical perturbations during active touch.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Proprioception is the sense of where the body or its parts are in space.
source: Proprioception is the sense of where the body or its parts are in space.
evidence: This is a definition based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: It is critical that the brain knows where in space the touched body part was at the time of contact to interpret touch.
source: To interpret touch, it is critical that the brain also knows where in space the touched body part was at the time of contact.
evidence: This is a statement based on established understanding of sensory processing.

claim: Touch and proprioception are intimately linked during normal sensory-motor function.
source: Thus, touch and proprioception are intimately linked during normal sensory-motor function.
evidence: This is an inference from the relationship between touch and body position awareness.

claim: Touch begins with the activation of low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs) in the skin.
source: Touch begins with the activation of low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs) in the skin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the sensory basis of touch.

claim: Information about body position can come from efference copy signals that report the motor commands ultimately used to control muscles.
source: Information about body position can come from efference copy signals that report the motor commands ultimately used to control muscles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about motor control and proprioception.

claim: The nervous system contains dedicated mechanoreceptive proprioceptor endings to provide feedback about actual, rather than intended, position.
source: However, the nervous system contains dedicated mechanoreceptive proprioceptor endings to provide feedback about actual, rather than intended, position.
evidence: This is established knowledge about proprioceptive sensory systems.

claim: Classical proprioceptors include muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ afferents.
source: Classical proprioceptors include muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ afferents.
evidence: This is established knowledge about proprioceptor types.

claim: Many rodents use rapid motions of their mystacial vibrissae (whiskers) to explore the tactile world.
source: Many rodents use rapid motions of their mystacial vibrissae (whiskers) to explore the tactile world (Carvell and Simons, 1990; Welker, 1964; Wineski, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The muscles controlling whisking motions lack classical proprioceptor endings.
source: Curiously, the muscles controlling these 'whisking' motions, as with other facial muscles, lack classical proprioceptor endings (Moore et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Feedback about whisker position must occur via self-motion-triggered activity of peripheral mechanoreceptors other than classical muscle proprioceptors.
source: Therefore, feedback about whisker position must occur via self-motion-triggered ('reafferent') activity of peripheral mechanoreceptors other than classical muscle proprioceptors, such as the cutaneous LTMRs responsible for sensing touch.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of classical proprioceptors in whisking muscles.

claim: Neurons throughout the whisker somatosensory system respond to whisker self-motion in a manner that depends on whisk phase.
source: Neurons throughout the whisker somatosensory system respond to whisker self-motion in a manner that depends on the relative position of the whisker within the current whisk cycle, or whisk 'phase' (Campagner et al., 2016; Crochet and Petersen, 2006; Curtis and Kleinfeld, 2009; Fee et al., 1997; Hires et al., 2015; Khatri et al., 2009; Leiser and Moxon, 2007; Moore et al., 2015; Severson et al., 2017; Szwed et al., 2003; Wallach et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2006; Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Whisk phase is thought to be a key coordinate system for whisker-based sensation.
source: Whisk phase is thought to be a key coordinate system for whisker-based sensation (Curtis and Kleinfeld, 2009; Kleinfeld and Deschênes, 2011; Szwed et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LTMRs that innervate the whisker follicles encode whisk phase and other aspects of whisker motion and touch during active sensing.
source: LTMRs that innervate the whisker follicles encode whisk phase and other aspects of whisker motion and touch during active sensing (Bush et al., 2016; Campagner et al., 2016; Khatri et al., 2009; Leiser and Moxon, 2007; Severson et al., 2017; Szwed et al., 2003; Szwed et al., 2006; Wallach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Whisker follicle LTMRs include Merkel-type endings, which are slowly adapting and thought to play a major role in perception of object shape and texture.
source: These LTMRs include Merkel-type endings, which are slowly adapting and thought to play a major role in perception of object shape and texture.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Merkel-type endings.

claim: Individual Merkel and unidentified slowly adapting whisker afferents respond both to touch and to self-motion.
source: Individual Merkel and unidentified slowly adapting whisker afferents respond both to touch and to self-motion (Severson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Self-motion (reafferent) responses arise from diverse mechanical sensitivities of whisker afferents.
source: Self-motion (reafferent) responses arise from diverse mechanical sensitivities of whisker afferents (Campagner et al., 2016; Severson et al., 2017; Wallach et al., 2016), and may be used by the brain for whisker proprioception (for behavioral studies addressing whisker proprioception, see: Knutsen et al., 2006; Mehta et al., 2007; O'Connor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Self-motion responses may be used by the brain for whisker proprioception.
source: Self-motion (reafferent) responses arise from diverse mechanical sensitivities of whisker afferents (Campagner et al., 2016; Severson et al., 2017; Wallach et al., 2016), and may be used by the brain for whisker proprioception (for behavioral studies addressing whisker proprioception, see: Knutsen et al., 2006; Mehta et al., 2007; O'Connor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Neurons in the brainstem with tactile receptive fields on parts of the face other than whiskers can respond during whisking in a manner that reports whisk phase.
source: Neurons in the brainstem (one synapse downstream from mechanoreceptors) with tactile receptive fields on parts of the face other than whiskers can also respond during whisking in a manner that reports whisk phase (Moore et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mechanoreceptors innervating facial parts other than whiskers could encode whisker motion, including whisk phase, but this has not been tested.
source: This suggests that mechanoreceptors innervating facial parts other than whiskers could encode whisker motion, including whisk phase, but this has not been tested.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from brainstem neuron responses and identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: 67 units were recorded from the trigeminal ganglion with whisker receptive fields.
source: We first analyzed units in the trigeminal ganglion (TG) with touch receptive fields confined to single whiskers (Figure 2A, n = 67).
evidence: This is a direct report of the number of units recorded in the experiments.

claim: Many whisker afferents were direction-selective, preferring manual deflections in either the protraction or retraction direction.
source: Many of these afferents were direction-selective, preferring manual deflections in either the protraction or retraction direction (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: 42 whisker afferents were whisking-sensitive.
source: A subset of these whisker afferents was more active during whisking (n = 42 'whisking-sensitive' units, defined in Glossary), consistent with prior work (see Materials and Methods for comparison to Szwed et al., 2003) and strongly modulated by phase, preferring to fire at a particular phase of the whisk cycle (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is a direct report of the number of whisking-sensitive units from the experimental data.

claim: Whisking-sensitive whisker afferents were strongly modulated by phase, preferring to fire at a particular phase of the whisk cycle.
source: A subset of these whisker afferents was more active during whisking (n = 42 'whisking-sensitive' units, defined in Glossary), consistent with prior work (see Materials and Methods for comparison to Szwed et al., 2003) and strongly modulated by phase, preferring to fire at a particular phase of the whisk cycle (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Sharp phase tuning of whisker afferents largely reflects sensitivity to inertial stresses.
source: This sharp phase tuning largely reflects sensitivity to inertial stresses (Severson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mutual information between phase and spike count for whisker afferents was 9.1 ± 23.8 bits/s (median ± IQR; n = 42 whisking-sensitive units).
source: Mutual information between phase and spike count for whisker afferents, expressed as an information rate via multiplying by the 500 Hz sampling frequency, was 9.1 ± 23.8 bits/s (median ± interquartile range [IQR]; n = 42 whisking-sensitive units).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Whisker afferent spike counts were better explained by phase (normalized MI = 0.096 ± 0.121) than by θ (0.034 ± 0.064), θ' (0.046 ± 0.086), θ'' (0.030 ± 0.076), θamp (0.012 ± 0.024), or θmid (0.0089 ± 0.013).
source: Whisker afferent spike counts were better explained by phase (Figure 2E; normalized MI = 0.096 ± 0.121; median ± IQR) than by θ (0.034 ± 0.064), θ' (0.046 ± 0.086), θ'' (0.030 ± 0.076), θamp (0.012 ± 0.024), or θmid (0.0089 ± 0.013; p < 0.0031 for all five comparisons, two-tailed K-S tests).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: 85 units were recorded from the trigeminal ganglion with touch receptive fields on hairy skin.
source: We began by recording from TG units with touch receptive fields on hairy skin (n = 85) rather than a vibrissa (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct report of the number of units recorded in the experiments.

claim: Hairy skin afferents responded to manual deflections of all small hairs or a small number of guard hairs within the mapped receptive field.
source: Afferents responded to manual deflections of all small hairs or a small number of guard hairs within the mapped receptive field, were rapidly adapting, and responded to touch in all directions (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Hairy skin afferents were rapidly adapting.
source: Afferents responded to manual deflections of all small hairs or a small number of guard hairs within the mapped receptive field, were rapidly adapting, and responded to touch in all directions (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Hairy skin afferents responded to touch in all directions.
source: Afferents responded to manual deflections of all small hairs or a small number of guard hairs within the mapped receptive field, were rapidly adapting, and responded to touch in all directions (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: 58 of 85 facial hairy skin afferents were whisking-sensitive.
source: Remarkably, activity of a large number of facial hairy skin afferents was modulated during whisking in air (Figure 3B; 58 of 85 were whisking-sensitive).
evidence: This is a direct report from the experimental data.

claim: Many facial hairy skin afferents fired at multiple phases of the whisk cycle.
source: Consistent with the lack of direction-selectivity, many facial hairy skin afferents fired at multiple phases (e.g. both protraction and retraction phases) of the whisk cycle (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Phase coding by hairy skin afferents varied by receptive field location, such that units with receptive fields closer to the whisker pad tended to encode phase more strongly than those distant from the pad.
source: Phase coding by hairy skin afferents varied by receptive field location, such that units with receptive fields closer to the whisker pad tended to encode phase more strongly than those distant from the pad (Figure 3D; overall MI rate = 1.3 ± 4.5 bits/s; median ± IQR).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Overall mutual information rate between phase and spike count for hairy skin afferents was 1.3 ± 4.5 bits/s (median ± IQR).
source: Phase coding by hairy skin afferents varied by receptive field location, such that units with receptive fields closer to the whisker pad tended to encode phase more strongly than those distant from the pad (Figure 3D; overall MI rate = 1.3 ± 4.5 bits/s; median ± IQR).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: 14 units had receptive fields on the whisker pad.
source: Units with receptive fields on the whisker pad (n = 14) were particularly modulated by phase (13 of 14 were whisking-sensitive).
evidence: This is a direct report from the experimental data.

claim: 13 of 14 whisker pad units were whisking-sensitive.
source: Units with receptive fields on the whisker pad (n = 14) were particularly modulated by phase (13 of 14 were whisking-sensitive).
evidence: This is a direct report from the experimental data.

claim: Receptive fields on the pad were smaller in area than other regions of the face.
source: Receptive fields on the pad were smaller in area than other regions of the face (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Pad hairy skin afferent encoding of phase (MI rate = 9.26 ± 8.53 bits/s, median ± IQR, n = 13) was comparable to whisker afferents.
source: Pad hairy skin afferent encoding of phase (MI rate = 9.26 ± 8.53 bits/s, median ± IQR, n = 13) was comparable to whisker afferents and significantly higher than afferents innervating hairy skin on the cheek (0.73 ± 2.10 bits/s, n = 18), eye (1.11 ± 3.57 bits/s, n = 10), lip (0.75 ± 1.76 bits/s, n = 5), snout (1.63 ± 1.23 bits/s, n = 9), and jaw (0.08 ± 0.09 bits/s, n = 3; Figure 3E; p < 0.032 for all five two-tailed K-S tests).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Pad hairy skin afferent encoding of phase was significantly higher than cheek afferents (0.73 ± 2.10 bits/s, n = 18).
source: Pad hairy skin afferent encoding of phase (MI rate = 9.26 ± 8.53 bits/s, median ± IQR, n = 13) was comparable to whisker afferents and significantly higher than afferents innervating hairy skin on the cheek (0.73 ± 2.10 bits/s, n = 18), eye (1.11 ± 3.57 bits/s, n = 10), lip (0.75 ± 1.76 bits/s, n = 5), snout (1.63 ± 1.23 bits/s, n = 9), and jaw (0.08 ± 0.09 bits/s, n = 3; Figure 3E; p < 0.032 for all five two-tailed K-S tests).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Pad hairy skin afferent encoding of phase was significantly higher than eye afferents (1.11 ± 3.57 bits/s, n = 10).
source: Pad hairy skin afferent encoding of phase (MI rate = 9.26 ± 8.53 bits/s, median ± IQR, n = 13) was comparable to whisker afferents and significantly higher than afferents innervating hairy skin on the cheek (0.73 ± 2.10 bits/s, n = 18), eye (1.11 ± 3.57 bits/s, n = 10), lip (0.75 ± 1.76 bits/s, n = 5), snout (1.63 ± 1.23 bits/s, n = 9), and jaw (0.08 ± 0.09 bits/s, n = 3; Figure 3E; p < 0.032 for all five two-tailed K-S tests).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Pad hairy skin afferent encoding of phase was significantly higher than lip afferents (0.75 ± 1.76 bits/s, n = 5).
source: Pad hairy skin afferent encoding of phase (MI rate = 9.26 ± 8.53 bits/s, median ± IQR, n = 13) was comparable to whisker afferents and significantly higher than afferents innervating hairy skin on the cheek (0.73 ± 2.10 bits/s, n = 18), eye (1.11 ± 3.57 bits/s, n = 10), lip (0.75 ± 1.76 bits/s, n = 5), snout (1.63 ± 1.23 bits/s, n = 9), and jaw (0.08 ± 0.09 bits/s, n = 3; Figure 3E; p < 0.032 for all five two-tailed K-S tests).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Pad hairy skin afferent encoding of phase was significantly higher than snout afferents (1.63 ± 1.23 bits/s, n = 9).
source: Pad hairy skin afferent encoding of phase (MI rate = 9.26 ± 8.53 bits/s, median ± IQR, n = 13) was comparable to whisker afferents and significantly higher than afferents innervating hairy skin on the cheek (0.73 ± 2.10 bits/s, n = 18), eye (1.11 ± 3.57 bits/s, n = 10), lip (0.75 ± 1.76 bits/s, n = 5), snout (1.63 ± 1.23 bits/s, n = 9), and jaw (0.08 ± 0.09 bits/s, n = 3; Figure 3E; p < 0.032 for all five two-tailed K-S tests).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Pad hairy skin afferent encoding of phase was significantly higher than jaw afferents (0.08 ± 0.09 bits/s, n = 3).
source: Pad hairy skin afferent encoding of phase (MI rate = 9.26 ± 8.53 bits/s, median ± IQR, n = 13) was comparable to whisker afferents and significantly higher than afferents innervating hairy skin on the cheek (0.73 ± 2.10 bits/s, n = 18), eye (1.11 ± 3.57 bits/s, n = 10), lip (0.75 ± 1.76 bits/s, n = 5), snout (1.63 ± 1.23 bits/s, n = 9), and jaw (0.08 ± 0.09 bits/s, n = 3; Figure 3E; p < 0.032 for all five two-tailed K-S tests).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Across all facial hairy skin afferents, normalized MI was significantly higher for phase (0.0165 ± 0.0348) compared to θ' (0.0062 ± 0.0098), θ'' (0.0056 ± 0.0098), θamp (0.0085 ± 0.012), and θmid (0.0094 ± 0.011).
source: Across all facial hairy skin afferents, normalized MI (Figure 3F) was significantly higher for phase (0.0165 ± 0.0348) compared to θ' (0.0062 ± 0.0098), θ'' (0.0056 ± 0.0098), θamp (0.0085 ± 0.012), and θmid (0.0094 ± 0.011; p < 0.003 for all four two-tailed K-S tests), but similar to θ (0.014 ± 0.023; p = 0.77, two-tailed K-S test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Across all facial hairy skin afferents, normalized MI for phase was similar to θ (0.014 ± 0.023).
source: Across all facial hairy skin afferents, normalized MI (Figure 3F) was significantly higher for phase (0.0165 ± 0.0348) compared to θ' (0.0062 ± 0.0098), θ'' (0.0056 ± 0.0098), θamp (0.0085 ± 0.012), and θmid (0.0094 ± 0.011; p < 0.003 for all four two-tailed K-S tests), but similar to θ (0.014 ± 0.023; p = 0.77, two-tailed K-S test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Widespread patterns of skin strain likely occur in a manner correlated with whisking, with stronger correlations between skin and whisker displacements occurring for facial regions on or near the whisker pad.
source: Video capturing facial motion and whisker position suggested that widespread patterns of skin strain likely occur in a manner correlated with whisking, with stronger correlations between skin and whisker displacements occurring for facial regions on or near the whisker pad (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from video analysis presented in the supplementary figure.

claim: The vibrissae above the eye whisk in phase with the whiskers.
source: In addition to skin movements, we observed that the vibrissae above the eye whisk in phase with the whiskers.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Mice have several vibrissae outside of the mystacial pad, including two supraorbital vibrissae above the eye, one genal vibrissa on the cheek, and several microvibrissae on the upper lip.
source: Mice have several vibrissae outside of the mystacial pad, including two supraorbital vibrissae above the eye, one genal vibrissa on the cheek (Danforth, 1925), and several microvibrissae on the upper lip (Figure 4A; Brecht et al., 1997).
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Non-mystacial vibrissa sinus follicle structures are highly conserved within strains of mice.
source: These sinus follicle structures are highly conserved within strains of mice (Dun and Fraser, 1958) and are present in many mammals (Danforth, 1925; Grant et al., 2013; Wineski, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Non-mystacial vibrissa sinus follicle structures are present in many mammals.
source: These sinus follicle structures are highly conserved within strains of mice (Dun and Fraser, 1958) and are present in many mammals (Danforth, 1925; Grant et al., 2013; Wineski, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Supraorbital vibrissae moved in phase with the whiskers.
source: Supraorbital vibrissae (Figure 4B–D; Video 3) and the genal vibrissa (Figure 4B–D; Video 4) moved in phase with the whiskers.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data and videos.

claim: The genal vibrissa moved in phase with the whiskers.
source: Supraorbital vibrissae (Figure 4B–D; Video 3) and the genal vibrissa (Figure 4B–D; Video 4) moved in phase with the whiskers.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data and videos.

claim: Microvibrissa barely moved.
source: Microvibrissa barely moved (Figure 4B–D; Video 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data and videos.

claim: Some instances of 'missed' whisk cycles occurred, in which the whisker moved, but the supraorbital or genal vibrissae remained still.
source: We observed some instances of 'missed' whisk cycles, in which the whisker moved, but the supraorbital or genal vibrissae remained still (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Adjacent whiskers correlated almost perfectly (Pearson's correlation coefficient, r = 0.98 ± 0.03, n = 14 recordings from 11 mice) with no phase lag (0.00 ± 0.03 radians).
source: Adjacent whiskers correlated almost perfectly (Pearson's correlation coefficient, r = 0.98 ± 0.03, n = 14 recordings from 11 mice) with no phase lag (0.00 ± 0.03 radians).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Supraorbital vibrissae movements correlated strongly with whisker movements (r = 0.78 ± 0.07, mean ± SD, n = 6 recordings from six mice), but with a short phase lag (Φlag = 0.27 ± 0.05 radians, mean ± SD).
source: Supraorbital vibrissae movements correlated strongly with whisker movements (r = 0.78 ± 0.07, mean ± SD, n = 6 recordings from six mice), but with a short phase lag (Figure 4C–E; Φlag = 0.27 ± 0.05 radians, mean ± SD; p = 4.9e-12, one-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Whisking amplitude was smaller for supraorbital vibrissae (4.7 ± 2.1°, mean ±SEM) compared to whiskers (12.5 ± 2.5°, mean ± SEM).
source: Whisking amplitude (θamp) was smaller for supraorbital vibrissae (4.7 ± 2.1°, mean ±SEM) compared to whiskers (Figure 4F; 12.5 ± 2.5°, mean ± SEM; p = 1.1e-6, one-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Genal vibrissa motion correlated strongly with that of the whiskers (r = 0.83 ± 0.08, mean ± SD), but with a longer phase lag (Φlag = 0.61 ± 0.18 radians, mean ± SD).
source: Genal vibrissa motion also correlated strongly with that of the whiskers (r = 0.83 ± 0.08, mean ± SD), but with a longer phase lag (Figure 4C–E; Φlag = 0.61 ± 0.18 radians, mean ± SD; p = 9.9e-11, one-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Whisking amplitude for genal vibrissae was smaller (2.2 ± 1.4°, mean ±SEM) compared to the tracked whiskers and supraorbital vibrissae.
source: Whisking amplitude for genal vibrissae was also smaller (2.2 ± 1.4°, mean ±SEM) compared to the tracked whiskers (Figure 4F; p = 6.9e-9, one-tailed t-test) and supraorbital vibrissae (p = 0.016, one-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Microvibrissae motion correlated with whisker motion less well (r = 0.27 ± 0.29, mean ± SD, n = 3 recordings from three mice) with a short delay (Φlag = 0.44 ± 0.11 radians, mean ± SD).
source: Microvibrissae motion correlated with whisker motion less well (r = 0.27 ± 0.29, mean ± SD, n = 3 recordings from three mice) with a short delay (Figure 4C–E; Φlag = 0.44 ± 0.11 radians, mean ± SD; p = 4.8e-10, one-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Whisking amplitude for microvibrissae (0.84 ± 0.23°, mean ± SEM) was smaller than for whiskers and supraorbital vibrissae.
source: Whisking amplitude for microvibrissae (Figure 4F, 0.84 ± 0.23°, mean ± SEM) was smaller than for whiskers (p = 3.5e-7, one-tailed t-test) and supraorbital vibrissae (p = 0.0086, one-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Lesioning the buccal branch of the left facial nerve abolished whisking of the mystacial whiskers on the left side (mean whisker θamp reduced from 11.2 ± 4.6° to 0.4 ± 0.2°, mean ± SEM, n = 6 videographic recordings).
source: We then lesioned the buccal branch of the left facial nerve, which innervates the mystacial pad (Dörfl, 1985; Fee et al., 1997). As expected, this manipulation abolished whisking of the mystacial whiskers on the left side (mean whisker θamp reduced from 11.2 ± 4.6° to 0.4 ± 0.2°, mean ± SEM, n = 6 videographic recordings), while leaving whisking intact on the right side (Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1I; Video 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental manipulation.

claim: Whisking of the supraorbital vibrissae was intact after buccal cut (supraorbital θamp: 4.2 ± 2.4° vs 4.9 ± 2.8°, n = 3 recordings), despite the abolished whisker motion.
source: Whisking of the supraorbital vibrissae was intact after buccal cut (supraorbital θamp: 4.2 ± 2.4° vs 4.9 ± 2.8°, n = 3 recordings), despite the abolished whisker motion (Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1I; Video 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental manipulation.

claim: Genal vibrissae showed a reduction in θamp after buccal cut (genal θamp: 2.2 ± 1.3° vs 0.8 ± 0.5°, n = 3 recordings).
source: In contrast, genal vibrissae showed a reduction in θamp after buccal cut (genal θamp: 2.2 ± 1.3° vs 0.8 ± 0.5°, n = 3 recordings; Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1J; Video 7).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental manipulation.

claim: Subsequent cut of the left facial nerve at the junction of the temporal and zygomatic branches eliminated whisking of the left supraorbital vibrissae (supraorbital θamp: 0.08 ± 0.05°, n = 3 recordings).
source: Subsequent cut of the left facial nerve at the junction of the temporal and zygomatic branches (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G) eliminated whisking of the left supraorbital vibrissae (supraorbital θamp: 0.08 ± 0.05°, n = 3 recordings; Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental manipulation.

claim: Genal vibrissae motion is passive or dependent on the buccal innervation of the whisker pad.
source: Thus, genal vibrissae motion is passive or dependent on the buccal innervation of the whisker pad, whereas whisking by the supraorbital vibrissae is active and under neuromuscular control separate from the mystacial whiskers.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the nerve lesion experiments.

claim: Whisking by the supraorbital vibrissae is active and under neuromuscular control separate from the mystacial whiskers.
source: Thus, genal vibrissae motion is passive or dependent on the buccal innervation of the whisker pad, whereas whisking by the supraorbital vibrissae is active and under neuromuscular control separate from the mystacial whiskers.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the nerve lesion experiments.

claim: 8 of 17 supraorbital vibrissa units were whisking-sensitive.
source: We found units, some of which were active during whisking, on supraorbital vibrissae (8 of 17 whisking-sensitive), genal vibrissae (3 of 8 whisking-sensitive), and microvibrissae (8 of 10 whisking-sensitive).
evidence: This is a direct report from the experimental data.

claim: 3 of 8 genal vibrissa units were whisking-sensitive.
source: We found units, some of which were active during whisking, on supraorbital vibrissae (8 of 17 whisking-sensitive), genal vibrissae (3 of 8 whisking-sensitive), and microvibrissae (8 of 10 whisking-sensitive).
evidence: This is a direct report from the experimental data.

claim: 8 of 10 microvibrissa units were whisking-sensitive.
source: We found units, some of which were active during whisking, on supraorbital vibrissae (8 of 17 whisking-sensitive), genal vibrissae (3 of 8 whisking-sensitive), and microvibrissae (8 of 10 whisking-sensitive).
evidence: This is a direct report from the experimental data.

claim: Supraorbital afferents encoded similar amounts of information about phase (MI rate = 16.2 ± 14.9 bits/s, median ± IQR) as genal afferents (5.2 ± 8.6 bits/s, median ± IQR).
source: Supraorbital afferents encoded similar amounts of information about phase (MI rate = 16.2 ± 14.9 bits/s, median ± IQR) as genal afferents (5.2 ± 8.6 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 0.23, two-tailed K-S test), and more than microvibrissa afferents (Figure 4J; 0.74 ± 1.60 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 0.0014, two-tailed K-S test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Supraorbital afferents encoded more information about phase than microvibrissa afferents (0.74 ± 1.60 bits/s, median ± IQR).
source: Supraorbital afferents encoded similar amounts of information about phase (MI rate = 16.2 ± 14.9 bits/s, median ± IQR) as genal afferents (5.2 ± 8.6 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 0.23, two-tailed K-S test), and more than microvibrissa afferents (Figure 4J; 0.74 ± 1.60 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 0.0014, two-tailed K-S test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The spike counts of non-mystacial vibrissa afferents overall were better explained by Φ (normalized MI = 0.062 ± 0.17, median ± IQR) and θ (0.047 ± 0.042) compared to θamp (0.019 ± 0.034), and θmid (0.021 ± 0.033).
source: The spike counts of non-mystacial vibrissa afferents overall were better explained by Φ (Figure 4K; normalized MI = 0.062 ± 0.17, median ± IQR) and θ (0.047 ± 0.042) compared to θamp (0.019 ± 0.034), and θmid (0.021 ± 0.033; p < 0.049 for all four two-tailed K-S tests).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: MeV neurons respond to aspects of whisker motion.
source: Recently, it has been suggested that MeV neurons respond to aspects of whisker motion (Mameli et al., 2010; Mameli et al., 2014; Mameli et al., 2017), which necessitates their inclusion in a full account of possible sources of peripheral information about whisker motion available to the brain (Bosman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 23 putative jaw muscle proprioceptors were recorded in MeV.
source: For analysis we considered both these putative jaw muscle proprioceptors (n = 23 units), plus units that were recorded on the same tetrode as a putative proprioceptor (n = 20 units) and therefore also presumably in MeV.
evidence: This is a direct report from the experimental data.

claim: 33 MeV units were whisking-sensitive.
source: MeV units (n = 33 whisking-sensitive) were not tuned to whisk phase (Figure 5D) and thus did not encode much information about phase (0.04 ± 0.04 bits/s, median ± IQR).
evidence: This is a direct report from the experimental data.

claim: MeV units were not tuned to whisk phase and did not encode much information about phase (0.04 ± 0.04 bits/s, median ± IQR).
source: MeV units (n = 33 whisking-sensitive) were not tuned to whisk phase (Figure 5D) and thus did not encode much information about phase (0.04 ± 0.04 bits/s, median ± IQR).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Only 2 of 33 whisking-sensitive MeV units had MI confidence intervals for Φ above chance levels.
source: Overall, only 2 of 33 whisking-sensitive MeV units (both putative jaw proprioceptors) had MI confidence intervals for Φ above chance levels (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: A correlation was observed between MeV activity and whisking midpoint.
source: However, we did observe a correlation between MeV activity and whisking midpoint (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: 18 of 33 whisking-sensitive MeV units had MI confidence intervals for θmid above chance levels.
source: Eighteen of 33 whisking-sensitive MeV units (including 15 out of 23 putative proprioceptors) had MI confidence intervals for θmid above chance levels (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Units that most strongly encoded θmid were putative jaw proprioceptors.
source: Units that most strongly encoded θmid were putative jaw proprioceptors (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data analysis.

claim: MI values between spike count and slowly varying kinematic quantities were low for MeV units (e.g. θmid: 0.17 ± 0.38 bits/s, median ± IQR).
source: However, MI values between spike count and these slowly varying quantities were low (e.g. θmid: 0.17 ± 0.38 bits/s, median ± IQR).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: MeV activity is not correlated with whisk phase.
source: Thus, MeV activity is not correlated with whisk phase and appears only weakly correlated with whisking midpoint.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data analysis.

claim: MeV activity appears only weakly correlated with whisking midpoint.
source: Thus, MeV activity is not correlated with whisk phase and appears only weakly correlated with whisking midpoint.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The weak correlation between MeV activity and whisking midpoint may be explained by slight changes in jaw position associated with whisking around more or less protracted midpoints.
source: We speculate that this weak correlation may be explained by slight changes in jaw position associated with whisking around more or less protracted midpoints.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Non-mystacial vibrissae afferents best encoded θmid (MI rate = 0.81 ± 1.80 bits/s, median ± IQR) as a population.
source: Overall, as a population the non-mystacial vibrissae afferents best encoded θmid (Figure 6A; MI rate = 0.81 ± 1.80 bits/s, median ± IQR), with similar encoding by whisker afferents (0.68 ± 1.08 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 0.28, two-tailed K-S test vs non-mystacial afferents) and facial hairy skin afferents (0.72 ± 1.16 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 0.61, two-tailed K-S test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Whisker afferents encoded θmid similarly (0.68 ± 1.08 bits/s, median ± IQR) to non-mystacial vibrissae afferents.
source: Overall, as a population the non-mystacial vibrissae afferents best encoded θmid (Figure 6A; MI rate = 0.81 ± 1.80 bits/s, median ± IQR), with similar encoding by whisker afferents (0.68 ± 1.08 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 0.28, two-tailed K-S test vs non-mystacial afferents) and facial hairy skin afferents (0.72 ± 1.16 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 0.61, two-tailed K-S test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Facial hairy skin afferents encoded θmid similarly (0.72 ± 1.16 bits/s, median ± IQR) to non-mystacial vibrissae afferents.
source: Overall, as a population the non-mystacial vibrissae afferents best encoded θmid (Figure 6A; MI rate = 0.81 ± 1.80 bits/s, median ± IQR), with similar encoding by whisker afferents (0.68 ± 1.08 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 0.28, two-tailed K-S test vs non-mystacial afferents) and facial hairy skin afferents (0.72 ± 1.16 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 0.61, two-tailed K-S test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: MeV spike counts encoded θmid less well (0.17 ± 0.38 bits/s, median ± IQR) than all other afferent classes.
source: MeV spike counts encoded θmid less well than all other afferent classes (0.17 ± 0.38 bits/s, median ± IQR; p < 6.7e-4 for all three two-tailed K-S tests).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Phase was best encoded by whisker (MI rate = 9.1 ± 23.8 bits/s, median ± IQR) and non-mystacial vibrissae afferents (2.9 ± 11.9 bits/s, median ± IQR).
source: Phase was best encoded by whisker (Figure 6C; MI rate = 9.1 ± 23.8 bits/s, median ± IQR) and non-mystacial vibrissae afferents (2.9 ± 11.9 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 0.15, two-tailed K-S test vs whisker) compared with facial hairy skin afferents (1.3 ± 4.5 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 3.0e-5, two-tailed K-S test vs whisker) and MeV afferents (0.04 ± 0.04 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 8.9e-16, two-tailed K-S test vs whisker).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Facial hairy skin afferents encoded phase less well (1.3 ± 4.5 bits/s, median ± IQR) than whisker afferents.
source: Phase was best encoded by whisker (Figure 6C; MI rate = 9.1 ± 23.8 bits/s, median ± IQR) and non-mystacial vibrissae afferents (2.9 ± 11.9 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 0.15, two-tailed K-S test vs whisker) compared with facial hairy skin afferents (1.3 ± 4.5 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 3.0e-5, two-tailed K-S test vs whisker) and MeV afferents (0.04 ± 0.04 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 8.9e-16, two-tailed K-S test vs whisker).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: MeV afferents encoded phase less well (0.04 ± 0.04 bits/s, median ± IQR) than whisker afferents.
source: Phase was best encoded by whisker (Figure 6C; MI rate = 9.1 ± 23.8 bits/s, median ± IQR) and non-mystacial vibrissae afferents (2.9 ± 11.9 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 0.15, two-tailed K-S test vs whisker) compared with facial hairy skin afferents (1.3 ± 4.5 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 3.0e-5, two-tailed K-S test vs whisker) and MeV afferents (0.04 ± 0.04 bits/s, median ± IQR; p = 8.9e-16, two-tailed K-S test vs whisker).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Normalized mutual information values showed that phase better explained the spike count of whisker afferents (0.096 ± 0.121, median ± IQR) compared with facial hairy skin (0.017 ± 0.035, median ± IQR), non-mystacial vibrissae (0.062 ± 0.166, median ± IQR), and MeV afferents (6e-4 ± 10e-4, median ± IQR).
source: Similarly, normalized mutual information values showed that phase better explained the spike count of whisker afferents (Figure 6C; 0.096 ± 0.121, median ± IQR) compared with facial hairy skin (0.017 ± 0.035, median ± IQR; p = 1.0e-10, two-tailed K-S test), non-mystacial vibrissae (0.062 ± 0.166, median ± IQR; p = 0.02, two-tailed K-S test), and MeV afferents (6e-4 ± 10e-4, median ± IQR; p = 8.9e-17, two-tailed K-S test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Mutual information between phase and spike count was similar for whisker (9.1 ± 23.8 bits/s), pad (9.3 ± 8.5 bits/s, median ± IQR), and supraorbital mechanoreceptors (16.2 ± 14.9 bits/s).
source: Mutual information between phase and spike count was similar for whisker (Figure 6D; n = 42; 9.1 ± 23.8 bits/s), pad (n = 13; 9.3 ± 8.5 bits/s, median ± IQR), and supraorbital mechanoreceptors (n = 8; 16.2 ± 14.9 bits/s; p > 0.11 for all three two-tailed K-S tests), and negligible for jaw proprioceptors (n = 23; 0.04 ± 0.04 bits/s; p < 8.4e-6 for all three two-tailed K-S tests).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Mutual information between phase and spike count was negligible for jaw proprioceptors (0.04 ± 0.04 bits/s).
source: Mutual information between phase and spike count was similar for whisker (Figure 6D; n = 42; 9.1 ± 23.8 bits/s), pad (n = 13; 9.3 ± 8.5 bits/s, median ± IQR), and supraorbital mechanoreceptors (n = 8; 16.2 ± 14.9 bits/s; p > 0.11 for all three two-tailed K-S tests), and negligible for jaw proprioceptors (n = 23; 0.04 ± 0.04 bits/s; p < 8.4e-6 for all three two-tailed K-S tests).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Whisker mechanoreceptors as a group best encode whisk phase.
source: Thus, while whisker mechanoreceptors as a group best encode whisk phase, mechanoreceptors with receptive fields on whisker pad hairy skin and on the supraorbital vibrissae also send to the brain a signal that encodes whisk phase (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Mechanoreceptors with receptive fields on whisker pad hairy skin also send to the brain a signal that encodes whisk phase.
source: Thus, while whisker mechanoreceptors as a group best encode whisk phase, mechanoreceptors with receptive fields on whisker pad hairy skin and on the supraorbital vibrissae also send to the brain a signal that encodes whisk phase (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Mechanoreceptors with receptive fields on the supraorbital vibrissae also send to the brain a signal that encodes whisk phase.
source: Thus, while whisker mechanoreceptors as a group best encode whisk phase, mechanoreceptors with receptive fields on whisker pad hairy skin and on the supraorbital vibrissae also send to the brain a signal that encodes whisk phase (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The strong phase coding observed in prior work with whisker afferents could serve as a basis for whisker proprioception.
source: Thus, our results support the hypothesis that the strong phase coding observed in prior work with whisker afferents (Campagner et al., 2016; Severson et al., 2017; Szwed et al., 2003; Wallach et al., 2016) could serve as a basis for whisker proprioception.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: Skin strain occurring within the receptive field, and in a pattern correlated with whisker motion, underlies the self-motion responses of facial hairy skin afferents.
source: While passive or active touch of the whiskers did not strongly activate facial hairy skin mechanoreceptors, passive stretch of the skin within or near their receptive fields was sufficient to cause spiking (not shown). This suggests that skin strain occurring within the receptive field, and in a pattern correlated with whisker motion, underlies the self-motion responses of these afferents.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Pad mechanoreceptor responses could provide the brain with reference signals to use in interpreting incoming touch responses from whisker afferents.
source: Pad mechanoreceptor responses could provide the brain with reference signals to use in interpreting incoming touch responses from whisker afferents.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Pad afferents encoded the angular position and velocity of the whiskers, kinematic variables that can be used in combination with stresses induced by whisker touch to compute both the azimuthal and radial location of objects.
source: For example, pad afferents encoded the angular position and velocity of the whiskers, kinematic variables that can be used in combination with stresses induced by whisker touch to compute both the azimuthal and radial location of objects (Birdwell et al., 2007; Knutsen and Ahissar, 2009; Mehta et al., 2007; Solomon and Hartmann, 2011; Szwed et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and the experimental data.

claim: Pad afferents may play a role in supporting redundant methods for object localization.
source: Pad afferents may thus play a role in supporting redundant methods for object localization.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Cutaneous afferents have been reported to be active during self-motion in systems other than the whisker system.
source: Cutaneous afferents have been reported to be active during self-motion in systems other than the whisker system.
evidence: This is established knowledge that will be supported by subsequent citations.

claim: During jaw movements in rabbits, non-direction-selective hairy skin afferents were found to respond to self-motion in a manner proportional to movement speed.
source: During jaw movements in rabbits, non-direction-selective hairy skin afferents were found to respond to self-motion in a manner proportional to movement speed (Appenteng et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In humans, microneurography studies have reported activity in cutaneous afferents related to movement of the face, ankle, knee, and finger.
source: In humans, microneurography studies have reported activity in cutaneous afferents related to movement of the face (Johansson et al., 1988), ankle (Aimonetti et al., 2007), knee (Edin, 2001), and finger (Edin and Abbs, 1991; Hulliger et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 'Cutaneous' (reafferent) signals of potential use for proprioception occur across a wide variety of body parts and animal species.
source: Thus, 'cutaneous' (reafferent) signals of potential use for proprioception occur across a wide variety of body parts and animal species.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited studies.

claim: In rodents, major aspects of the structure and innervation of the supraorbital and genal vibrissae closely resemble those of mystacial vibrissae.
source: In rodents, major aspects of the structure and innervation (Fundin et al., 1995; Wineski, 1985) of the supraorbital and genal vibrissae closely resemble those of mystacial vibrissae (Fundin et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Motions of non-mystacial vibrissae were assessed in the golden hamster, and they were found to be relatively immobile.
source: Motions of these non-mystacial vibrissae were assessed in the golden hamster, and they were found to be relatively immobile (Wineski, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In opossum, the genal vibrissae were observed to be mobile, contain intrinsic protractor muscles, and move in phase with mystacial whiskers.
source: In opossum, the genal vibrissae were observed to be mobile, contain intrinsic protractor muscles, and move in phase with mystacial whiskers (Grant et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In mice the supraorbital and genal vibrissae are mobile and move in phase with mystacial whiskers.
source: Here, we show that in mice the supraorbital and genal vibrissae are indeed mobile and move in phase with mystacial whiskers.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Supraorbital vibrissae whisking motion is under active neuromuscular control and persists after cutting the motor nerve that drives whisking of the mystacial whiskers.
source: In the case of the supraorbital vibrissae, we confirm that this whisking motion is under active neuromuscular control and persists after cutting the motor nerve that drives whisking of the mystacial whiskers.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental manipulation.

claim: The observation of tight coupling of whisker and non-mystacial vibrissa movements adds to our understanding of the exquisitely coordinated orofacial motor actions in rodents.
source: The observation of tight coupling of whisker and non-mystacial vibrissa movements adds to our understanding of the exquisitely coordinated orofacial motor actions in rodents (Kurnikova et al., 2017; Welker, 1964) and suggests that their premotor circuits are linked (Deschênes et al., 2016; Kleinfeld et al., 2014; McElvain et al., 2018; Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The tight coupling of whisker and non-mystacial vibrissa movements suggests that their premotor circuits are linked.
source: The observation of tight coupling of whisker and non-mystacial vibrissa movements adds to our understanding of the exquisitely coordinated orofacial motor actions in rodents (Kurnikova et al., 2017; Welker, 1964) and suggests that their premotor circuits are linked (Deschênes et al., 2016; Kleinfeld et al., 2014; McElvain et al., 2018; Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Supraorbital and genal vibrissae afferents displayed strong phase tuning and carried information about phase comparable to that of whisker afferents.
source: Afferents with receptive fields on these structures, especially the supraorbital and genal vibrissae, displayed strong phase tuning and carried information about phase comparable to that of whisker afferents.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Supraorbital and genal vibrissae are unlikely to contact objects that are in reach of the whiskers.
source: While the supraorbital and genal vibrissae afferents encoded the phase of the whiskers in the whisk cycle, these non-mystacial vibrissae are unlikely to contact objects that are in reach of the whiskers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical location of these vibrissae.

claim: Afferents with non-mystacial vibrissae receptive fields could provide the brain with a phase signal that is unperturbed by contacts between whiskers and objects in the world.
source: Thus, an interesting possibility is that afferents with non-mystacial vibrissae receptive fields could provide the brain with a phase signal that is, unlike that of touch-sensitive whisker afferents we report here and in past work (Severson et al., 2017), unperturbed by contacts between whiskers and objects in the world.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: It will be important to determine whether the strong correlations in phase between non-mystacial vibrissae and whiskers generalize across behavioral conditions.
source: It will be important to determine whether the strong correlations in phase we observed between non-mystacial vibrissae and whiskers generalize across behavioral conditions, such as during behavioral tasks in freely moving animals.
evidence: This identifies a direction for future research.

claim: Tasks that require highly precise information about the phase of a particular whisker to be combined with touch signals may require direct sensing of phase by afferents innervating that whisker itself.
source: Moreover, tasks that require highly precise information about the phase of a particular whisker to be combined with touch signals may require direct sensing of phase by afferents innervating that whisker itself.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Whisker afferents that respond to whisking in air but not touch have been found, and could serve the role of separating contact from phase signals with high precision.
source: Whisker afferents that respond to whisking in air but not touch have been found (Szwed et al., 2003), and could serve the role of separating contact from phase signals with high precision.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and includes speculation about function.

claim: The coding of whisker self-motion occurs via a multitude of sensory signals arising from distinct classes of facial mechanoreceptors.
source: We conclude that the coding of whisker self-motion occurs via a multitude of sensory signals arising from distinct classes of facial mechanoreceptors.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the experimental data.
